query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin, reactive nickel interlayer on tungsten particles before spark‐plasma sintering will create graded, Ni‐rich interfacial phases that enhance Cu wettability, reduce interfacial voids, and improve mechanical durability under high-irradiation, high-heat-flux conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite material consisting of connected tungsten particles within a copper matrix intended for fusion reactor joint applications.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin nickel coating to tungsten particles via electroless plating prior to spark‐plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Sintering conducted at temperatures between 1200–1400 °C under a controlled vacuum or inert atmosphere; tested under simulated irradiation and thermal cycling conditions representative of fusion reactor service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Ni-rich intermetallic phases formed at the W/Cu interface during sintering.
generation.mechanism: The deposited Ni layer reacts during sintering to form a graded intermetallic that improves the wetting of copper on tungsten, thereby reducing voids and phase separation. This improved interfacial contact is expected to enhance thermal transport and maintain mechanical integrity under service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline produced without an interlayer (e.g., the vapor-coated tungsten powders sintered directly with copper), the nickel-treated composite will exhibit lower porosity at W/Cu interfaces, enhanced thermal conductivity, and superior mechanical durability under cyclic irradiation and thermal loads.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication methods such as vapor-coating of tungsten powders followed by sintering without the tailored interfacial treatment.
generation.boundary: Processing must be kept below tungsten’s melting point, and the composite must withstand fusion-reactor joint service conditions, including high irradiation doses and thermal cycling.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in thermal transport and mechanical durability, as well as long-term behavior of the Ni-induced intermetallic phases under extended irradiation, remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of W-Cu composites: one where tungsten particles are pre-coated with a thin nickel layer and a control group without the nickel interlayer. Process both by spark-plasma sintering under identical conditions. Subject the samples to accelerated thermal cycling and irradiation relevant to fusion reactor joints.
measurements: High-resolution microscopy (SEM/TEM) to assess the interfacial microstructure and quantify voids
Thermal conductivity tests to measure improvements in heat transport
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., tensile/compression tests) before and after irradiation/thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nickel-treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in interfacial void formation, improvement in thermal conductivity, or enhanced mechanical durability compared to the control group, or if detrimental interfacial phases form, then the hypothesis is falsified.
